s: Kai lives with his dad. That is two people. Lena lives with her mom, dad, and four sisters. Both are families. A *family* is a group of people who belong together and care for each other. It can be small or big.
m: Families can grow. A new baby may be born. A grandpa may come to live at home. Families can also get smaller when someone moves far away. Through all of that, the people still care for each other.

s: Rosa's Aunt Luz is her mom's sister. Uncle Tom is married to Aunt Luz. Their children, Ben and Mia, are Rosa's *cousins*. A cousin is the child of your aunt or uncle. Your uncle is your parent's brother.
m: Cousins can be very close, almost like friends. They may have the same grandma and grandpa. That is why they often meet at big family meals. Some cousins are about your age. Others are much older or younger.

s: Grandma Ana lives in Mexico with her son and his children. She makes tortillas, and her grandson Luis likes to flip them. Each age group in a family is a *generation*. Grandparents, parents, and children are three generations. Homes like this are found in Mexico, India, Italy, Korea, and Chicago.
m: Living together can help everyone. In a home with three generations, there are many people to help. A grandparent may be home when a child comes back from school. A child may help with a small job. People share meals, space, and time.

s: Grandparents share what they know. In Korea, a grandmother may teach a child to fold dumplings. In Italy, a grandfather may show how to plant tomatoes. They pass on a *tradition*, a way a family does things for a long time. Children help too: they carry bags and listen.
m: Some traditions are stories. A grandparent may tell what life was like when they were young. Other traditions are songs or recipes. When a child learns one, it lives on. One day that child may teach it to someone else.

s: After dinner at Rosa's house, Dad washes the dishes, Rosa dries them, and Ben puts the cups away. Soon the sink is empty. A *chore* is a job you do at home. When everyone helps, the work goes fast.
m: Chores change as you grow. A small child can put toys in a box. An older child can help cook or fold clothes. Doing a chore also teaches you things, and it feels good to finish a job.

s: Mia's family eats pancakes on Saturday. Lena's family sings before dinner. Each family has its own ways, called *customs*. A custom is something a family does again and again. No custom is the only right one. When a friend tells about theirs, you can listen.
m: Customs can be big or small. One family may dance at a birthday. Another may read a story at bedtime. What makes a custom special is that the family does it together, again and again.

s: Yuki lives in Tokyo, Japan, on the tenth floor. She lives in an *apartment*, a home inside a bigger building. Many families live in one building. Big cities have lots of people and not much land. So people build tall buildings, up and not out.
m: An apartment building has stairs, and often an elevator. Your neighbors live close by, above you and below you. In a city, you can often walk to a store or a park.

s: Niran lives in Thailand, near a river. In the rainy season, the river rises and water spreads over the ground. His house stands on *stilts*, tall, strong poles. Water flows under the house, so his floor stays dry.
m: Stilts also let air move under a house. That can help keep the rooms cooler on hot, wet days. A stilt house is built to fit a place where the water rises and falls with the seasons.

s: Eva lives in New Mexico, where the sun is hot and there is little rain. Her home has thick walls made of *adobe*, a brick of mud and straw dried in the sun. The thick walls warm up slowly, so the inside stays cool.
m: Mud-brick homes are found in many dry parts of the world, not only in New Mexico. Some old mud-brick buildings are still standing after hundreds of years. Builders use earth from close by, so they do not have to carry materials far.

s: Bat's family are *herders* in Mongolia. They take care of sheep, goats, and horses. The animals need fresh grass, so the family moves. Their home is a ger, also called a yurt. Felt walls and a stove keep it warm. It can be taken down and put up again.
m: The felt in a ger is made from sheep wool. The wool is pressed and rolled with water until the fibers lock together into thick cloth. That cloth is strong, warm, and light enough to carry. Herders have used gers for a very long time.

s: Long ago, some Inuit hunters in the far north traveled in winter. At night they needed a shelter, a place safe from wind and cold. They cut hard snow into blocks and stacked them in a dome. This snow house is often called an *igloo*. Today, most Inuit live in wood houses.
m: Snow works well for building because it is full of tiny pockets of air. Air does not let heat pass through easily, so warmth stays in and cold stays out. That is why a snow dome with a small lamp can be warmer inside than the air outside.

s: Anna lives on a farm in the Swiss mountains. Lots of snow falls in winter, so her farmhouse has a steep roof. The snow slides off. In some old farmhouses, the house and barn were under one roof. In Europe, farmhouses may be stone or wood. Each one fits its land and weather.
m: In summer, some Swiss farm families take their cows up the mountain to eat fresh green grass. In winter, the cows stay in the barn. A farm family's work changes with the seasons.

s: A ger, an apartment, and a stilt house look different. Each gives *shelter* from wind, rain, and cold. A home needs clean water close by. Most of all, people in a home care for each other. Bat's new place was home because his family was there.
m: A home is also a place to keep your things and to rest after the day. Homes can be small or big. A home can be a house, an apartment, a boat, or a tent. What matters is that it keeps you safe and that you belong there.
